rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning and textual form of ʾīlāf in both verses are uncertain.
rows.anchor: Im Hinblick auf den Ausdruck ʾīlāf in V. 1 und 2 besteht sowohl textkritische als auch semantische Unsicherheit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the long alif in both verses and the yāʾ in verse 2 were added to the rasm, verse 2 could in principle be read ʾilf.
rows.anchor: dem traditionellen rasm zufolge in beiden Versen nur nachträglich in den Konsonantenduktus eingetragen wurde

rows.speaker: Jeffery und Birkeland
rows.claim: They report Ibn Masʿūd variants li-yaʾlafa and li-taʾlafa for verse 1.
rows.anchor: Jeffery und Birkeland zufolge werden für V. 1 von Ibn Masʿūd u. a. auch

rows.speaker: Birkeland
rows.claim: Birkeland reconstructs li-yaʾlafa Quraysh / ʾilfahum as the original wording, later changed to the received text in Medina; Paret criticizes this account.
rows.anchor: Birkeland nimmt deshalb als ursprünglichen Wortlaut an li-yaʾlafa Quraiš / ʾilfahum

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin corrects the reported Ibn Masʿūd form to la-yaʾlaf or la-taʾlaf, with lām al-amr, meaning Quraysh should remain devoted to worship as they remain devoted to the seasonal journey.
rows.anchor: Rubin weist jedoch darauf hin, dass die Ibn Masʿūd zugeschriebene Variante eigentlich la-yaʾlaf

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin considers that imperative variant a secondary product of theological reflection because early scholars could not accept divine favor toward Quraysh before their conversion.
rows.anchor: Rubin hat sicherlich recht damit, dass diese Lesart Produkt theologischer Reflexion und somit sekundär ist

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The received majority reading repeats ʾīlāf in both verses; Quranic repetition across consecutive verses supports it, as in other passages.
rows.anchor: Für die traditionelle Mehrheitsversion, die zweimal ʾīlāf liest, spricht überdies, dass die Wiederaufnahme eines Wortes im Folgevers ein koranisches Stilmittel ist

rows.speaker: Crone
rows.claim: Crone argues that most traditions about Quraysh protection pacts called ʾīlāf are later exegetical speculation, and their historical basis is doubtful.
rows.anchor: Wie Crone (1987, 204–214) herausgearbeitet hat, dürfte es sich bei einem Großteil der im Zusammenhang mit Q 106:1.2 überlieferten Traditionen um nachträgliche exegetische Spekulationen handeln

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the treaty traditions cannot be verified as historical knowledge, the expression should be interpreted through its root meaning.
rows.anchor: Eine kontrollierbare Deutung des Ausdrucks kann deshalb nur durch Ableitung von der Wurzelbedeutung versucht werden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alifa means either being connected with something or becoming accustomed to it; form IV can mean joining things or habituating someone to a thing or place.
rows.anchor: Alifa kann sowohl „verbunden sein mit“ als auch „sich gewöhnen an“ bedeuten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Western translations generally choose the sense of joining or bringing together, as in Paret’s rendering of Quraysh bringing the two journeys together.
rows.anchor: Die erste Alternative ist die in westlichen Koranübersetzungen gängige

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin argues for the alternative, also found in Islamic commentary, that Quraysh is the first object of ʾīlāf rather than its subject: their habituation to the winter and summer journey.
rows.anchor: Uri Rubin auf überzeugende Weise dafür plädiert, auch die in der obigen Übersetzung zugrunde gelegte Alternative zu erwägen

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin gives ʾīlāf a more specific sense of enabling habitual travel to a place in full protection and removing the hardship of doing so.
rows.anchor: seems to have a more specific meaning of enabling someone to resort habitually to a place under complete protection

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: In his 2011 revision, Rubin reads the journeys disapprovingly: Quraysh are compulsively preoccupied with worldly gain outside Mecca while neglecting the Kaaba’s Lord and their religious duties.
rows.anchor: Rubin allerdings weitgehend Abstand von dieser früheren Deutung

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revised reading detaches the sura from its close stylistic and traditional connection to 105, and assimilates its specific message to later passages in an anachronistic way.
rows.anchor: Problematisch hieran ist allerdings, dass ein solches Verständnis den Text inhaltlich ganz und gar von Sure 105 ablöst

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds it surprising that Neuwirth adopts Rubin’s revised reading while still describing 106 as a close text about divine favors following 105, since the interpretations conflict.
rows.anchor: Umso erstaunlicher ist deshalb, dass Neuwirth – die Q 106 ebenfalls zu den frühesten Koransuren rechnet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial li may express exclamation without criticizing the journeys: wonder at their regular success can lead into a call to thank God, the Lord of the House.
rows.anchor: Rubins Gedanke, das einleitende li- sei als lām li-t-taʿaǧǧub aufzufassen, durchaus einleuchtend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bait refers to the Kaaba, which is already called the House in the early Meccan passage 52:4.
rows.anchor: Als bait wird die Kaʿba frühmekkanisch noch in 52:4 bezeichnet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title Lord of this House parallels the Nabataean title mrʾ bytʾ for Dushara, supporting the view that the praised deity was originally a local Meccan protective god, consistent with Islamic tradition.
rows.anchor: Die Parallele bestätigt die durchaus mit der islamischen Tradition kongruente Ansicht, dass es sich bei der gepriesenen Gottheit um eine ursprünglich im mekkanischen Lokalkult verwurzelte Schutzgottheit handelt

rows.speaker: Andrae
rows.claim: Andrae says Christian poets identified the Kaaba’s god with the Christian God and could therefore join its cult as worship directed to him.
rows.anchor: Andrae weist darauf hin, „dass die christlichen Dichter den Gott der Kaʿba als den christlichen Gott betrachtet haben

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Andrae cites ʿAdī b. Zaid swearing in one breath by the Lord of Mecca and by the Crucified.
rows.anchor: so schwört etwa ʿAdī b. Zaid in einem Atemzug „beim Herrn Mekkas“ (wa-rabbi Makkata) und dem Gekreuzigten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the relation between the name Allah and the title Lord used here, the commentary refers to its note on 95:8.
rows.anchor: Zum Verhältnis des Gottesnamens Allāh zu dem hier gebrauchten Titel „Herr“ vgl. die Anmerkung zu 95:8

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Himṣ, Mecca, and Medina verse-counting traditions divide after hunger, that pause breaks the rhyme, and the verse is short enough to stand as the closing verse; Neuwirth rejects the division.
rows.anchor: Das so entstehende Versende stimmt jedoch nicht mit dem Reimschema überein

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here āmana means to grant security, its original Arabic sense; the later sense believe, borrowed from Northwest Semitic, becomes dominant afterward.
rows.anchor: Das Verb ʾāmana hat hier noch seine genuin arabische Bedeutung „Sicherheit gewähren“

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura is one four-verse syntactic unit with a monorhyme and consonant variation, chiefly fricatives.
rows.anchor: Die Sure besteht nur aus einem einzigen, vier Verse umfassenden Satzzusammenhang und weist einen Monoreim mit Konsonantenwechsel

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Because God is called Lord of the House in verse 3, the sura highlights Quraysh’s special status as residents of the Meccan sanctuary and their sacral inviolability among other tribes.
rows.anchor: Vor dem Hintergrund von V. 3, wo Gott als „Herr dieses Hauses“ (= der mekkanischen Kaʿba) beschrieben wird

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like 105, the sura concerns God’s special protection of the Meccan sanctuary and calls Quraysh to gratitude for it.
rows.anchor: Die Sure ist damit wie Q 105 dem besonderen Schutz gewidmet, den Allāh dem mekkanischen ḥaram gewährt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–2 state the reason for thanks in a prepositional phrase about the journeys; verse 3 calls for worship in the jussive, and verse 4 expands and motivates this with a hymn-like relative clause summarizing God’s favors.
rows.anchor: V. 3 schließt einen jussivischen Aufruf zur Gottesverehrung an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause resembles 96:1,4 formally, but that passage instead emphasizes God’s universal role as creator and revealer.
rows.anchor: Ein formal ähnlicher, jedoch inhaltlich ganz anders gelagerter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura has a two-step syllogistic structure: verses 1–2 state a fact, and verses 3–4 derive Quraysh’s duty to thank God from it.
rows.anchor: Die Sure weist so eine syllogismusartige Zweitaktigkeit auf: V. 1 und 2 beschreiben eine Tatsache

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from perfect-tense report to behavioral command also occurs in 93 from verse 9 and 94 from verse 7, and with a jussive in 108 from verse 1.
rows.anchor: Dieser Übergang vom Faktischen zum Normativen bzw. von der literarischen Form des im Perfekt

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin no longer wholly rejects the historicity of protection agreements, noting that references to the Quraysh pacts as ʾīlāf occur in lexicographical and historical rather than exegetical works, against Crone’s view of them as speculation.
rows.anchor: Obwohl Rubin ʾīlāf in V. 1.2 im Sinne von „gewöhnen an, ermöglichen“ deutet

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin interprets the shared root with the treaty name as wordplay: unreliable earthly pacts are superseded by a divine ʾīlāf that firmly secures Quraysh’s safety and welfare.
rows.anchor: On the contrary, it seems that by using the root ‚a.l.f.’, the Quran intends to suggest that instead of the earthly pacts with the tribes

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin traces recognition of the sanctuary and Mecca’s pilgrimage-center role, including markets such as ʿUkāẓ and economic benefit, to the failed Abraha attack in 105, which established Mecca’s sacred inviolability.
rows.anchor: Die Anerkennung des mekkanischen ḥaram und seiner Stellung als wichtiges Pilgerzentrum

rows.speaker: Peters
rows.claim: Peters suggests the winter and summer journeys may have been seasonal pilgrimages to the sanctuary rather than trading journeys; under either view their precise nature is secondary to the sura’s theology.
rows.anchor: Peters (1999, xxxvi) zu bedenken, dass es hierbei auch um saisonale Pilgerfahrten zum mekkanischen Heiligtum gehandelt haben könnte

rows.speaker: Birkeland
rows.claim: Birkeland states that the Lord, rather than circumstances, human skill, or covenants themselves, accounts for Quraysh’s favorable position.
rows.anchor: Not circumstances, not human skill, not covenants per se, but the Lord is the source of the favourable position of Quraiš

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike 105, 106 explicitly states the cultic duty arising from God’s favor: the beneficiaries should worship the Lord of this House, like the comfort suras 93, 94, and 108.
rows.anchor: Im Unterschied zu Q 105 werden dabei die sich aus Gottes Zuwendung ergebenden kultischen Verpflichtungen der von ihm Begünstigten explizit gemacht

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is not named explicitly in the first half, the audience likely already had a rudimentary awareness of receiving Allah’s special favors.
rows.anchor: Die Tatsache, dass Gott, das eigentliche Subjekt von V. 1.2, in der ersten Texthälfte gar nicht explizit erwähnt wird

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As 10:22–23 illustrates, the Quran radicalizes diffuse prior religious beliefs; Ammann rightly warns against treating revelation as the historically necessary completion of pre-Islamic monotheistic development.
rows.anchor: Wie auch in der späteren Stelle 10:22.23 deutlich wird, radikalisiert der Koran hier religiöse Überzeugungen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An explicit confession of monotheism belongs only to later texts, contrary to Rubin’s claim.
rows.anchor: Ein ausdrückliches Bekenntnis zum Eingottglauben ist allerdings erst späteren Texten vorbehalten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical phrase ʾa-raʾaita is compared with its repeated use in 96:9–13 and with 53:33–34.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary directs readers to notes on other uses of kaḏḏaba in 95:7, 92:16, and 73:11.
rows.anchor: Zu den verschiedenen Gebrauchsweisen von kaḏḏaba vgl. die Anmerkungen zu 95:7, 92:16 und 73:11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early Meccan dīn and yawm al-dīn are objects of belief or denial, supporting the received bi-d-dīn reading over Ibn Masʿūd’s variant without bi.
rows.anchor: Ad-dīn bzw. yaum ad-dīn erscheinen frühmekkanisch vor allem als Gegenstand des Glaubens

rows.speaker: Birkeland
rows.claim: Birkeland proposes that dīn means religion here rather than judgment, but the author rejects this because dīn and yawm al-dīn are synonymous prepositional objects of kaḏḏaba in Quranic usage.
rows.anchor: Birkelands Hypothese, dīn werde in 107:1 nicht in der Bedeutung von „Gericht“

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that early Meccan dīn generally means judgment, against Nöldeke and Schwally’s apparent translation as religion.
rows.anchor: Dīn dürfte deshalb frühmekkanisch generell mit „Gericht“ zu übersetzen sein

rows.speaker: Birkeland
rows.claim: Birkeland argues judgment would not fit because Muhammad still joined pre-Islamic Meccan prayer, but the author says cult separation could have followed the establishment of judgment themes.
rows.anchor: Auch Birkelands Gedanke, dass in Q 107 die Bedeutung „Gericht“ noch nicht sinnvoll sei

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn later means religion, as in 109:6; its early eschatological sense reflects Aramaic dīnā, while interference from Middle Persian dēn later supplied the religious sense.
rows.anchor: Der Hintergrund für diese Bedeutungsverschiebung ist in der komplexen Etymologie des Wortes zu suchen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift was not purely linguistic: judgment receded as a comprehensive religious system developed, allowing the Quranic word to take on the Persian-influenced sense of religion.
rows.anchor: Denn das koranische Wort dīn konnte nach seiner zunächst ausschließlich eschatologischen Verwendung wohl nur deshalb überhaupt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A probably authentic poem by Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt already uses dīn to mean religion, so Persian influence did not introduce that sense as a lexical innovation in Medinan suras.
rows.anchor: Ein interessantes Schlaglicht auf die vorkoranische Semantik von dīn ergibt sich aus einem wahrscheinlich authentischen Gedicht Umayya b. abī ṣ-Ṣalts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 2–3 parallel the vice catalogue in 89:17–18, which condemns neglect of orphans and the poor, devouring inheritance, and love of wealth; an alternate reading occurs for the exhortation to feed the poor.
rows.anchor: Vgl. den zu V.2.3 parallelen Teil des Lasterkatalogs in 89:17.18

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Food, orphans, and the poor recur together in the virtue list 90:13–16, with orphans and poor in 89:17–18, 93:9, 69:34, and 74:44, forming an early Quranic social-critical topos.
rows.anchor: Es handelt sich dabei also um einen schon früh im Koran auftretenden sozialkritischen Topos

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan and widow and the poor and wretched are stereotyped pairings in the Hebrew Bible, with examples in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Malachi, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.
rows.anchor: Auf ähnlich stereotype Weise können in der hebräischen Bibel „Witwe und Waise“

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The New Testament likewise commends charity and feeding the poor, especially Matthew 25, where these acts are placed in an eschatological setting like this sura.
rows.anchor: Die Verdienstlichkeit karitativer Taten und insbesondere der Speisung von Armen wird aber auch im Neuen Testament betont

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The notes also refer readers to related material on 93:9, 90:11–16, and the prophetic-ethical command to give full measure in 83:1–4.
rows.anchor: S. a. die Anmerkungen zu 93:9 und zu 90:11–16

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although yadaʿu from waḍaʿa is also transmitted, the majority yaduʿʿu is preferable because “shove away” is harsher and better fits the context and the following geminated root ḥaḍḍa.
rows.anchor: Für die Mehrheitslesung yaduʿʿu spricht jedoch, dass das schärfere „wegstoßen“ inhaltlich angemessener scheint

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root s-h-w here likely means the same as the later frequent term ghafla, religious heedlessness and negligence condemned also by Ephrem, according to Andrae; compare 51:11.
rows.anchor: der u. a. bei Ephrem verurteilten religiösen Sorglosigkeit und Nachlässigkeit entspricht

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ṣallā and ṣalāh, the notes refer to the discussion under 108:2.
rows.anchor: Zu ṣallā und ṣalāh vgl. die Anmerkung zu 108:2

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damascus, Mecca, and Medina verse counts do not end a verse after yurāʾūn; Neuwirth considers this formally plausible because 83:1–3 similarly has a short woe introduction followed by two longer vice-catalogue verses.
rows.anchor: formkritisch ist dies deshalb plausibel, weil auch in dem Wehspruch 83:1–3 auf einen kürzeren Einleitungsvers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If verses 6–7 are combined despite the rhyme potential at yurāʾūn, the sura has a symmetrical structure of two triads.
rows.anchor: so ergibt sich für Sure 107 ein symmetrischer Aufbau von zwei Dreiergruppen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura systematically links religious beliefs and ritual actions with an individual’s moral conduct in daily life.
rows.anchor: Die Sure etabliert systematisch einen Konnex zwischen religiösen Überzeugungen und kultischen Handlungen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first group uses a question introduced by ʾa-raʾaita to elicit the listener’s position on deniers of judgment, perhaps addressing worshippers who themselves observe the conduct in verses 4–5.
rows.anchor: Die erste Versgruppe tut dies in Form einer mit ʾa-raʾaita eingeleiteten Frage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer equates deniers of judgment with people who push orphans away and do not urge others to feed the poor.
rows.anchor: Die in V. 2.3 gegebene Antwort setzt die Leugner des Gerichts dann mit Menschen gleich

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awareness of the eschaton grounds social solidarity, a theme also found in 92:5–9; 104:1–3 depicts conduct when this eschatological awareness is absent.
rows.anchor: V. 1–3 stellen damit die beständige Gewärtigung des eschaton als Voraussetzung gesellschaftlicher Solidarität dar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This future-oriented accountability complements 106’s past-oriented grounding of present ethics in God’s earlier favors.
rows.anchor: komplementiert die Vergangenheitsorientierung der früheren Sure 106

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening divine first-person plural resembles 97:1, while 94:1 also opens with a divine address framed as a question.
rows.anchor: Vgl. die ebenfalls unmittelbar mit göttlicher Wir-Rede einsetzende Sure 97

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kauṯar is an adjective meaning abundant or plentiful, supported by a poetic use for a mass of dust and lexicographical evidence.
rows.anchor: ist eigentlich ein Adjektiv und bedeutet ‚viel, reichlich, in Fülle’

rows.speaker: Luxenberg
rows.claim: Luxenberg reads kūṯar as an Arabized form of Syriac kuttārā and interprets it as the virtue of steadfastness.
rows.anchor: Luxenberg (2000, 304–310) liest kūṯar statt kauṯar und betrachtet dies als Arabisierung von syr. kuttārā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author objects that Syriac kattar means remain or continue, but kuttārā is attested only temporally as duration or a term, not as an ethical virtue; Luxenberg relies on dictionary entries rather than concrete Syriac texts.
rows.anchor: das Substantiv kuttārā offenbar nur im temporalen Sinne von „Dauer, Frist“ und nicht in ethischen Zusammenhängen als Tugendbegriff belegt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luxenberg’s emendation to kūṯar disrupts the received rhyme pattern 3KK3r, reducing rather than improving formal cohesion.
rows.anchor: Luxenbergs Emendation des Ausdrucks zu kūṯar zur Folge, dass der erste Vers das im textus receptus vorhandene Reimschema 3KK3r durchbrechen würde

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The traditional translation “abundance” should stand, supported by Nöldeke’s poetic attestation and the concrete relief from need in 93 and 94, including the material gift promised in 93:5.
rows.anchor: Angesichts der von Nöldeke angeführten Belegstelle aus der Dichtung ist deshalb an der traditionellen Übersetzung „Fülle“ festzuhalten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early exegetical identification of al-Kawthar as a river in paradise is later legendary embellishment, as Luxenberg correctly observes.
rows.anchor: Die schon in der frühen islamischen Exegese anzutreffende Erklärung des Ausdrucks als Name eines der Ströme des Paradieses wertet Luxenberg zu recht als spätere legendarische Ausschmückung

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction likely calls the Prophet to participate in pre-Islamic Meccan sacrifice; exegetes found this troubling and invented a sense of raising the hand to the throat during prayer, while an Eid-sacrifice reading is anachronistic for an early Meccan text.
rows.anchor: Die Aufforderung, der Prophet möge sich am vorislamischen mekkanischen Opferkultus beteiligen

rows.speaker: Luxenberg
rows.claim: Luxenberg emends wa-nḥar to wa-nǧar, deriving “remain” from Syriac ngar, but the author calls this arbitrary: naḥara meaning sacrifice is clear, naǧara is unattested, and ṣabara could fit the rhyme.
rows.anchor: Luxenbergs Emendation von wa-nḥar zu wa-nǧar mit der analog zu syr. ngar unterstellten Bedeutung „verharren“

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣallā also describes pre-Islamic Meccan cult practice in 107:4–6; it is a denominal verb from ṣalāt, which derives from Aramaic ṣloṯā, unlike a native Arabic word.
rows.anchor: Ṣallā ist zweifellos kein genuin arabisches Wort, sondern ein Denominativum zu ṣalāt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author treats sabbaḥa’s Quranic sense “praise” as likewise explicable through semantic interference from Syriac.
rows.anchor: vgl. auch das Verb sabbaḥa, dessen koranische Verwendung im Sinne von „loben, preisen“ ebenfalls nur durch semantische Interferenz des Syrischen erklärlich ist

rows.speaker: Spitaler
rows.claim: Spitaler proposes that Arabic ṣalāt arose from the Aramaic-matching plural ṣalawāt, from which an Aramaizing singular was subsequently formed.
rows.anchor: Wie Spitaler 1998, 194, betont, dürfte die unmittelbare Verbindung zum Aramäischen über den Plural ṣalawāt verlaufen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since ṣalāt is attested in pre-Islamic poetry, the borrowing must have occurred before the Quran.
rows.anchor: Da das Wort schon in der vorkoranischen Dichtung nachweisbar ist, muss die Entlehnung bereits in vorkoranischer Zeit stattgefunden haben

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In early Meccan texts ṣallā can indicate exemplary virtue (75:31, 87:15, 96:10), as well as cult participation in 108:2 and cult criticism in 107:4–6; later groups include al-muṣallūn alongside other participial group names.
rows.anchor: Im frühmekkanischen Koran bezeichnet das Verb ṣallā außer in 108:2 und der Kultkritik in 107:4–6 noch an drei weiteren Stellen eine exemplarische Tugend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the title rabb, the commentary refers to the note on 95:8.
rows.anchor: Zum Gottestitel rabb s. die Anmerkung zu 95:8

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the anecdotal early exegetical tradition about an identified opponent insulting Muhammad as sonless, Paret’s general reading—that the warning applies to anyone who hates the Prophet—is preferable.
rows.anchor: Gegenüber dieser für die frühe islamische Koranexegese charakteristisch anekdotischen Lesart

rows.speaker: Neuwirth
rows.claim: Neuwirth notes that shāniʾ echoes Psalmic laments about haters, including the listed Psalms.
rows.anchor: So hat Neuwirth (Frühmekkanische Suren, 108) auf den Anklang des Begriffs šāniʾ an psalmistische Klagen über Hasser hingewiesen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hater figure also appears in pre-Islamic poetry; ʿAbīd b. al-Abraṣ says a friend often becomes a hater.
rows.anchor: Die Gestalt des „Hassers“ begegnet allerdings auch in der altarabischen Dichtung

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat of being uprooted in ʾabtar has an intertextual dimension, compared by Kouriyhe with Psalm 52:7.
rows.anchor: Schließlich hat auch die dem Hasser mit dem Wort ʾabtar angedrohte Entwurzelung eine textreferentielle Dimension

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The historical identification of the hater and the accusation that Muhammad lacked male heirs is uncertain; the sura is best read typologically with 94 and 97 as a comfort saying, without requiring a concrete historical occasion.
rows.anchor: Aus textimmanenter Perspektive ist eine solche historische Konkretisierung jedoch unsicher

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 1 recalls an unspecified divine favor, verse 2 derives an obligation to join Meccan prayer and sacrifice, and verse 3 promises eventual triumph over haters, contrasting their threatened severance with the preacher’s abundance.
rows.anchor: V. 1 vergegenwärtigt dem Angeredeten einen früheren göttlichen Gnadenakt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suras 93, 94, and 108 likely are the earliest Quranic texts to address the preacher personally; generic second-person lessons elsewhere need not identify him, while these comfort suras and 97 authorize the earlier proclamations against hostile resistance.
rows.anchor: Die drei Trostsuren 93, 94 und 108 stellen sehr wahrscheinlich die frühesten Korantexte dar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comfort suras share terminology and structure with Psalms: Muhammad resembles the afflicted Psalmist but receives a direct divine response, granting him religious prestige.
rows.anchor: Schilderungen derartiger Anfeindungen sowie Bekundungen des zu ihrer Bewältigung befähigenden Gottvertrauens begegnen auch in zahlreichen Psalmen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across 93, 94, 108, and 105–106, historical contingencies become acts of divine generosity that call for human ethical and cultic response; this reverses the sacrificial logic in which humans initiate action and the deity responds.
rows.anchor: In den genannten Suren manifestiert sich damit ein Umdeutungsprozess, welcher zuvor als Sphären von Kontingenz angesehene Realitätsbereiche

rows.speaker: Ammann
rows.claim: Ammann characterizes old Arabian cult as humans offering to call on a deity as a purchasable helper; Labīd’s poem calls fear and praise the most profitable transaction in distress.
rows.anchor: Kultstätten sind Wunschstätten, an denen man opfert, um Gott um etwas anzurufen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction ʾabū plus genitive marks a person by a defining trait, as in “father of guests”; plural aṣḥāb plus genitive works similarly, for example in 85:4.
rows.anchor: Die Verbindung ʾabū + Substantiv im Genitiv dient dazu, jemanden als Besitzer einer bestimmten Eigentümlichkeit zu charakterisieren

rows.speaker: Horovitz
rows.claim: Horovitz suggests “Father of Flame” is not an actual name but a figurative kunya coined by the sura to mark its bearer as hellbound.
rows.anchor: Horovitz vermutet, dass die Wendung „Vater der Flamme“ (ʾabū lahab) „kein eigentlicher Name“ sei

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the figure is Muhammad’s uncle ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, his “Father of Flame” epithet likely arose after this sura; the phrase should be translated to retain its link to the fire imagery in verse 3.
rows.anchor: so dürfte der Beiname „Vater der Flamme“ ihm erst im Gefolge der vorliegenden Koransure beigelegt worden sein

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura may instead describe a generic archetypal damned man of flames, like the wretched one burning in 92:15; identifying him with ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā may be a later anecdotal development in early Quran reception.
rows.anchor: Keineswegs auszuschließen ist allerdings, dass sich die Sure ursprünglich gar nicht gegen eine bestimmte Einzelperson richtet

rows.speaker: Rubin
rows.claim: Rubin takes yad as merit, translating the line as Abū Lahab’s merits being lost, based on a report that ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā earned merit through a vow to tend al-ʿUzzā’s shrine.
rows.anchor: Rubin, der die Sure primär im Rückgriff auf außerkoranische Traditionen deutet, will yad im Sinne von „Verdienst“ verstehen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although yad can mean merit, Fischer’s synecdoche of Abū Lahab’s two hands for his whole person is more likely, since the dual fits poorly with an abstract meaning.
rows.anchor: doch ist August Fischers Verständnis der beiden Hände von ʾabū lahab“ als einer Synekdoche für die gesamte Person des Verfluchten wahrscheinlicher

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that repeating tabba makes the hands and the person distinct fails: the final phrase most likely emphatically repeats the curse.
rows.anchor: Das den Vers abschließende wa-tabba ist am ehesten als eine bekräftigende Wiederholung der vorangehenden Verwünschung aufzufassen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classical exegetes gloss tabba as either losing or perishing; Rubin sees “lose” as original and “perish” as secondary overlay, but that depends on his reading yad as merit.
rows.anchor: Das Verb tabba selbst wird von islamischen Exegeten sowohl mit ḫasira

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With Fischer’s synecdoche, both glosses are possible nuances rather than competing meanings.
rows.anchor: es handelt sich bei den beiden Glossen deshalb wohl eher um unterschiedliche semantische Nuancen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported reading wa-qad tabba by Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmaš, and Ubayy b. Kaʿb clarifies the ambiguous text secondarily; the received wa-tabba is the more difficult reading and should stand.
rows.anchor: Von Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmaš und Ubayy b. Kaʿb wird die Lesart wa-qad tabba überliefert

rows.speaker: Fischer
rows.claim: Fischer reads the second tabba as a past assertion that doom has already struck, intensifying the preceding curse; Paret instead favors emphatic repetition, comparable to qutila in 74:19–20.
rows.anchor: August Fischer übersetzt das zweite tabba nicht als Imprekativ
